value.overview: The Short-billed Pigeon (Patagioenas nigrirostris) is a medium-sized forest pigeon of southern Mexico, Central America, and northwestern South America. It is most often detected by its distinctive, far-carrying call rather than seen clearly, because it usually forages high in trees. The species feeds mainly on fruits, berries, and mistletoe, and is associated with humid tropical forest and wooded landscapes. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species found mainly in lowland and foothill habitats.
value.classification: The Short-billed Pigeon belongs to the pigeon and dove family Columbidae and the genus Patagioenas. It is closely related to other large New World pigeons, including the Ruddy Pigeon.
value.identification: This pigeon is generally slate-gray to purplish-gray, with darker wings and back and a relatively short, dark bill. The head and breast may show subtle wine-colored or violet tones, while the underparts are usually paler. Females are somewhat duller, and juveniles are browner with scaled-looking feathers. It can resemble the Ruddy Pigeon, but voice, bill shape, and habitat or elevation help separate the species. Its loud, high-pitched, complex call is often the best identification clue.
value.rangeHabitat: The Short-billed Pigeon ranges from southern Mexico through Central America to northwestern Colombia. It uses humid lowland and foothill forests, forest edges, second growth, plantations with mature trees, and other wooded habitats where fruiting trees are available. In Costa Rica, it occurs in both Caribbean and Pacific lowlands and foothills, including sites such as Arenal, La Selva, and the southern Pacific region. It is generally associated with lower elevations than the closely related Ruddy Pigeon, although their ranges can overlap.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident and non-migratory. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round, although local movements may follow fruit availability and seasonal changes in food resources.
value.breeding: The species usually nests in trees, placing a simple platform of sticks among branches. As in many pigeons, the clutch is typically a single white egg, and both parents probably share incubation and care of the young. Breeding may occur during more than one season across its broad tropical range, with timing varying geographically and according to rainfall and food availability. Detailed breeding observations are less numerous than for many familiar pigeon species.
value.dietFeeding: The Short-billed Pigeon feeds mainly in the canopy, taking fruits, berries, and mistletoe fruits. It may also consume other soft plant material and occasionally visit the ground or roadsides to obtain grit. Birds are often encountered singly or in pairs, moving quietly through fruiting trees. Because much of its feeding occurs high above the ground, observers may hear the species more often than they see it.
value.behavior: This pigeon is usually unobtrusive and spends much of its time in the forest canopy. It commonly travels alone or in pairs and gives a distinctive, loud call at intervals, sometimes from a concealed perch. When disturbed, it may fly strongly through the trees or away from the observer. Its combination of quiet canopy foraging and conspicuous vocalizations makes listening especially useful when surveying forests in Costa Rica.

conservation.populationTrend: Population trend is considered broadly stable.
